newsitem.title: GERMANY: Zaire military planning meeting enters third day.
newsitem.headline: Zaire military planning meeting enters third day.

text.p: A meeting of Western and African military leaders planning options for a possible mission to aid refugees in Zaire entered its third day on Sunday amid questions whether a mission would be launched.
Talks between nations interested in contributing to a mission lasted into early Sunday before ending at 0030 GMT.

The meeting was then resumed on Sunday at about 0800 GMT at the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart, a spokesman for the Canadian forces, which is leading the multi-national force planned for Zaire, told Reuters.
"Nothing yet has been finalised about military options," Canadian Navy Reserve Lieutentant Charles Brown said.

Military planners and aid groups at an initial meeting on Friday failed to agree on the number of refugees at risk. A Canadian military official said on Saturday the issue still dogged talks and declined to say whether progress was made.

"This is a very complex process," the Canadian official, who asked not to be identified, said of the talks led by Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, who is coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission.

Aid officials also ended one-day talks on Saturday in Geneva on central Africa's refugee crisis after also apparently failing to agree on how many refugees were on the move, where they are and whether foreign troops should go in to help them.
The Stuttgart meeting was expected to consider various military options but leave the final decision of a humanitarian relief mission to individual governments.

Three possible options in a preliminary discussion document seen by Reuters set out the pros and cons of basing a military relief operation in Rwanda or in Zaire and included a third option of not sending any extra troops at all.
In one option under discussion according to delegates at the meeting, external forces would maintain low-level operational help they now give to Rwanda and relief agencies.

Support for a planned task force in east Zaire has cooled with the return of hundreds of thousands of refugees to Rwanda and the United States opting not to commit combat troops. One European military official said momentum for the mission had waned.
"It seems as though a lot will favour keeping the status quo and not stepping up the commitment since the situation is starting to take care of itself," the official said.

Expectations for limited, if any, military action were underpinned by U.S. army officials in Africa saying on Saturday that a week-long assessment showed 202,000 refugees remained in eastern Zaire and many might decide not to return to Rwanda.

U.S. army Major-General Edwin Smith, leader of the U.S. team, denied the military was in any "contest for credibility" over numbers. But 202,000 was a third the number of refugees estimated by the U.N. refugee agency as still trapped in Zaire.
Smith said he did not want to influence the Stuttgart talks but some aid officials in Africa put the U.S. estimate in the context of a U.S. aim to avoid military intervention.
Briefing papers at the Stuttgart meeting have noted that many nations were ready to provide relief from a base in Rwanda, and the option would probably only need light security.

But it would require approval from Rwanda, which has so far been reluctant to see an operation on its soil. Providing relief from a Zairean base would mean having to establish a secure headquarters, probably with heavy forces.

The papers also said the idea had support from the Zairean government but carried a bigger risk of becoming embroiled in regional conflict. The option would also limit efforts to repatriate Hutu refugees who fled from Rwanda in 1994.
Such a mission would also need more complex logistical suppport than a Rwanda-based operation and take more time.
